SECONDARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM SHPT Sec-
ondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) in dialysis patients (see 
Figure 18.4) can progress to severe, intractable forms of bone
disease. Prolonged exposure to elevations of PTH causes the 
development of osteitis ﬁ brosa cystica, a form of bone disease
characterized by rapid bone turnover with an excess of col-
lagen production and inadequate mineralization. Although
bone mass itself may appear constant, bone quality is poor 
and the bones are more prone to fracture. Th e decrease in 
bone mineralization can cause vascular and soft tissue calci-
ﬁ cation. Patients at this stage often are resistant to vitamin D
therapy and require a surgical parathyroidectomy. Resistance 
to erythropoietin therapy, related to marrow ﬁ brosis, may also 
be noted in patients with SHPT. Once the disease progresses to 
advanced stages, irreversible changes usually have occurred in
the patient’s parathyroid glands, thus making this disease state 
diﬃ  cult to treat.
